title: Capron v. Van Noorden (1804)
summary: The losing plaintiff could obtain reversal because the record failed to establish the federal court’s subject-matter jurisdiction.
notes:
This very short assigned opinion concerns what the record established. It does not find that the parties in fact shared citizenship or resolve the substantive claim. The casebook’s questions ask why a losing plaintiff might seek reversal that produces no merits victory.

The action was one of trespass on the case in the federal circuit court for North Carolina; the record alleged only that Van Noorden was 'late of Pitt County' and said nothing about Capron's own citizenship, and the plaintiff who had lost on the merits successfully used the jurisdictional defect he himself had failed to plead to obtain reversal.

sections.Parties: Capron was the plaintiff in an action of trespass on the case. Van Noorden was the defendant. After losing, Capron himself challenged the federal court’s authority.
sections.Material Facts: The record described Van Noorden as late of Pitt County, North Carolina, but did not establish the citizenship needed for federal jurisdiction. In particular, it did not show the necessary relationship between the parties’ citizenship. Describing where a person has lived does not itself establish all jurisdictional facts. The action had already proceeded to a verdict for the defendant when the problem reached the Supreme Court.
sections.Procedural History: Capron brought the action in the federal circuit court in North Carolina. The defendant obtained a verdict and judgment. Capron sought review by writ of error, assigning the jurisdictional deficiency in the record as error. The Supreme Court reversed the judgment. Its disposition did not award Capron damages or decide the merits in his favor.
sections.Issue: Could the plaintiff who selected the federal forum challenge an adverse judgment when the record did not show that the court had jurisdiction?
sections.Holding: Yes. The Supreme Court reversed the judgment. The reported decision gives no reasons: the familiar statement that “it was the duty of the Court to see that they had jurisdiction, for the consent of parties could not give it” comes from Harper’s argument for the plaintiff in error, which the Court accepted by reversing.
sections.Reasoning: The report consists of Harper’s argument and a one-line disposition (“Judgment reversed”), so the reasoning later cases attribute to Capron is inferred from what the Court did. The principle the case stands for: a federal court’s subject-matter authority must appear on the record and exists independently of the parties’ willingness to litigate, so even the plaintiff who chose the forum may assign its want of jurisdiction as error. The decision separates the validity of the adjudicative process from the merits of the underlying wrong: a defendant’s favorable verdict cannot sustain a judgment when the record fails to establish federal jurisdiction. Rule 12(h)(3) states the modern form of the same rule.

learning.why: The losing plaintiff could obtain reversal because the record failed to establish the federal court’s subject-matter jurisdiction.

topics.cp-subject-matter: Capron requires the federal court to establish its own subject-matter authority even when the plaintiff chose that court.
topics.cp-waiver: Consent and the plaintiff’s own error cannot supply missing subject-matter jurisdiction.
topics.cp-procedure-merits: Reversal for a jurisdictional defect leaves the underlying claim undecided.
topics.cp-diversity: The missing jurisdictional fact was the parties' citizenship required for diversity.
topics.cp-citizenship: Alleging that a party was 'late of' a county did not plead the citizenship needed for diversity.
topics.cp-finality: A judgment on the merits was set aside because the jurisdictional defect could be raised even by the losing plaintiff.

mnemonic.rationale: A plaintiff who appealed his own case
